summary: Britain announced it will provide Ukraine with the technology to produce long-range Storm Shadow missiles locally, marking the effort as a step to address European production bottlenecks. In response, the Kremlin stated that Russian forces are actively working to locate these production sites and criticized London's involvement in the conflict. The announcement coincided with Ukraine's 35th independence anniversary, which was marked by visits from several international leaders, including the new British prime minister.
key_points: Britain's Defense Ministry announced plans to give Ukraine technology to produce Storm Shadow missiles domestically.
The Kremlin condemned the move, stating that Russian forces are working to identify the missile production sites.
France previously licensed Ukraine to produce identical SCALP missiles in July, though analysts note full-scale factories are required for such complex manufacturing.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited Kyiv on his first official trip to mark Ukraine's 35th independence anniversary.

title: Boy, 5, died after jumping from ‘compromised’ window in 15th-floor flat, coroner says
author: Jordan Reynolds
content:
A five-year-old boy died after jumping from a 15th-floor tower block window that was "compromised", a coroner said.
Aalim Ahmed was killed instantly in the fall from a tilt-and-turn kitchen window at a residential property in Plaistow, east London.
His distraught father, Makail Ahmed, rushed down from the top-floor temporary social housing flat and found his body shortly before 6am on May 16 2024.
Describing the death as "preventable", Aalim’s mother, Sahra Osman, blamed Newham Council, stating she had reported safety concerns about the home on multiple occasions.
Conflicting evidence regarding the condition of the window fittings was presented during the inquest into the young boy’s death.
An engineer dispatched by Newham Council to inspect and review overhauling the windows and handles told the court they were fully functional when he visited on December 17 2023.
However, the court heard that Ms Osman had submitted a series of complaints over several months, including fears that the windows opened too far and that she lacked a key.
Assistant coroner Ian Wade, sitting at East London Coroner’s Court, said the windows “were not used appropriately”.
He delivered a narrative conclusion on Monday, in which he said: “Aalim was an active five-year-old boy who suffered from a diagnosed condition called autism, such as to render him incapable of making reliable judgments about his personal safety and abilities.
“In the early hours of May 16 2024… he awoke and went from his bedroom to the kitchen, he climbed onto a chair and then onto the windowsill of an insecure double turn and tilt window.
“He opened the window and in a naive belief that he could fly or alternatively could come to no harm he leapt from the open window… he died at the scene.”
![Jacobs House in Plaistow, east London](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/24/18/c19e4b574583f0a9bc48bf240fc7e71fY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3Njc3NzY2-2.76191858.jpg)
Mr Wade said he did not find a basis for issuing a report to prevent future deaths, adding: “I find there was no compelling reason why a landlord should’ve considered that placing this little boy on the 15th floor was inappropriate.”
He said: “It wasn’t the fact that it was the 15th floor that was significant, what was significant was that the windows had become compromised.”
The court previously heard a young child’s voice is twice heard counting down “three, two, one” followed a few seconds later by “a loud clang” was captured on grainy audio, which was taken from CCTV outside the apartment block.
Detective Constable Joe Linton, who carried out a review of CCTV footage outside Jacobs House, previously said “it is most likely from the footage available” that Aalim had “jumped out” of the flat at the building in New City Road “of his own accord without the presence of a third party”.
A post-mortem examination found Aalim died from “multiple injuries due to or as a consequence of trauma” from a “fall from height”.
Ms Osman has told the court she was “scared” and “horrified” when the council put her young family in the flat, which needed repairs, saying Aalim was autistic with “no sense of danger”.
All the windows were closed before the family, which also included her toddler son and a newborn girl, went to bed.
Ms Osman denied any suggestion she may have “forced” the window open to cope in hot weather.
Aalim could have been climbing to get a biscuit from a cupboard but the windows had “faulty” restrictors and her ongoing complaints to get them fixed led only to a series of workmen who did not sort the problem, she said.
Window engineer Charlie Mann said the windows were “all working”, including the handles and restrictors, when he tested them in December 2023.
A restrictor is a safety device which is meant to allow the window to open only 50-100mm.
Having spoken to the mother, who said her son had autism, he decided the restrictors should be changed to a lockable version rather than one that can be worked by a button.
He ordered nine restrictors and contractors came to fix them in January 2024.
Charlie Mann’s father, James Mann, who is managing director of ABC Ltd the firm where the window engineer works, watched videos of police operating the window from which Aalim fell.
He said the window appeared to be going into “dual mode”, which he said could be caused by “misalignment, misuse or force”.
This is a fault which meant the window tilted and turned open at the same time, despite the handle being in only the tilt position.
In the video, the court saw that the restrictor did not engage every time the police officer tested the window.
He said that “there needs to be an adjustment, something is not quite right” but he added he needed to see more of the window to have a clearer idea of the problem.
Tom Monk, who worked for ABC Ltd, told the court he went to the flat in January 2024 to fit the new restrictors and spent one to two hours there.
He said he may have been there twice, a couple of days later and fitted a new hinge on a casement window.
Detective Inspector Jamie Humm, who investigated the incident, said there was “no evidence or suspicion he (Aalim) had been forced”.
“The flat was well furnished and it was clearly a loving environment for a child,” he noted.
He added that soon after arriving at the scene he was satisfied “there was no evidence of a crime, not that I thought there would be”.
John Gray, cabinet member for housing, Newham Council, said: “This was a tragic accident which resulted in the heartbreaking death of a young five-year-old child.
“Our thoughts continue to be with Aalim’s family and friends during this incredibly difficult time.
“We are grateful to the coroner Ian Wade KC for his thorough and fair hearing of the facts of this case, which have at times been very difficult to hear and revisit.”
summary: Five-year-old Aalim Ahmed died from multiple injuries after falling from a 15th-floor temporary social housing flat window in east London on May 16, 2024. An inquest heard that the autistic boy climbed onto a chair and the windowsill before jumping from the compromised tilt-and-turn window, believing he could fly. While the boy's mother blamed Newham Council and reported previous safety concerns regarding faulty windows, the coroner concluded the death was a tragic accident and did not issue a report to prevent future deaths.
key_points: Aalim Ahmed, a five-year-old autistic boy, died instantly after falling from a 15th-floor window in Plaistow, east London.
Assistant coroner Ian Wade delivered a narrative conclusion stating the child climbed onto the windowsill of an insecure window and jumped.
The boy's mother, Sahra Osman, had previously submitted complaints to Newham Council stating the windows opened too far and lacked proper security.
Conflicting evidence was presented at the inquest regarding the condition of the window fittings and whether the restrictors were fully functional.
Investigators found no evidence of third-party involvement or foul play, treating the incident as a tragic accident.

title: UK drone factories may face attacks from 'unknown sources' says Kremlin advisor
author: Helen Sullivan
content:
![Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky (R) and Prime Minister of Britain Andy Burnham (L) pose as they attend a signing documents ceremony during their meeting at the Presidential office in Kyiv, Ukraine, 24 August 2026, amid the ongoing Russian invasion.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/864d/live/f9140c60-a029-11f1-acc9-bb1a45146942.jpg)
- Published
Andrei Fedorov, an adviser to the Kremlin, says there might be a "semi-military" response against UK drone factories by "unknown sources" over the sharing military blueprints with Russia.
His comments on BBC Newsnight come as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he plans to travel to the US next month with European leaders to lobby US President Trump on Ukraine's defence needs.
In an interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said, "I'm looking forward to going to New York in September," when the UN General Assembly will meet.
He said that while the details were not "fully confirmed", it is "likely" he will go. The trip would be his first to the US since becoming prime minister in July.
"Leaving today, I'm quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks," he said following his official visit to Ukraine on Monday, during which he promised to continue pressuring Russia.
The UK has also agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile. The blueprints will allow Ukraine to produce the long-range weapon domestically.
Fedorov, who is Russia's former deputy foreign minister, said Putin was facing "serious" pressure "to undertake certain measures against UK". Asked on BBC Newsnight where the pressure was coming from, Fedorov responded, "public opinion polls, it's coming from journalists, from mass media".
Asked what a "semi-military" response might look like, Fedorov said "it could take the form of something might happen with enterprises, with factories which are producing drones for Ukraine."
"They could be attacked not by Russia, but by from unknown sources," he said.
The comments are in line with those made by Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday, when he criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints. Peskov said it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace.
He told reporters on Monday that the Russian military was already gathering data to locate any missile production sites to destroy them.
"Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added.
In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?"
Burnham's visit to Ukraine was his first official international visit. He met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.
Burnham has been reaffirming the UK's support for Ukraine in the wake of escalating Russian strikes in recent weeks - including one last week on a shopping centre that killed at least 16 people.
Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriot interceptor missiles, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles, but stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks.
Zelensky has said he is hoping to secure 300 patriot missiles ahead of winter, when Russia is likely to increase its attacks on energy infrastructure, as it has done in past years.
In the interview with Bloomberg, Burnham said that he felt "really confident" that the issue was "fixable". But he pointed out that it wasn't only the US who could supply Ukraine with Patriots.
"There are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with," he said. "It's probably going to be a solution that involves a lot of layers and a lot of negotiation."
In July this year, three weeks after offering Ukraine the right to produce Patriots itself, Trump backtracked, saying, "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology."
"These weapons are incredible. We have to be very careful about letting somebody build them," Trump told a cabinet meeting.
In a joint statement after the meeting in Ukraine, Burnham and co-chairs French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the group would aim to strength Kyiv's air defences "as a matter or urgent priority".
They also condemned Moscow's "systemic and escalating strikes against Ukraine's cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and pledged to "constrain Russia's war chest through sanctions and actions against the "shadow fleet".
In a statement ahead of the visit, Burnham said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.
"I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."
He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."
summary: A Kremlin adviser warned that UK drone factories could face attacks from "unknown sources" in response to the UK sharing military blueprints with Ukraine. Meanwhile, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited Kyiv to pledge continued support and announced plans to lobby US President Trump for defense aid. The UK and its allies have also agreed to share missile component blueprints to help Ukraine produce long-range weapons domestically.
key_points: A Kremlin adviser stated that UK drone factories might face "semi-military" attacks from "unknown sources" over the UK sharing military blueprints with Russia.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited Kyiv on his first official international trip to reaffirm support for Ukraine.
The UK has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made missile components so Ukraine can produce long-range weapons domestically.
Burnham plans to travel to the US in September to meet European leaders and lobby President Trump regarding Ukraine's defense needs.

title: Suspected burglar charged over death of great-grandmother
author: Tom McArdle
content:
![Rose Smith, 75, died in hospital following a break-in at her north London home](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499416927_17875662273790_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq5YrzcumTXZZ7ZolnNshsm5Qd0gUcdddCv0EDOkSO7vg.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Rose Smith, 75, died in hospital following a break-in at her north London home](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499416927_17875662273790_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq5YrzcumTXZZ7ZolnNshsm5Qd0gUcdddCv0EDOkSO7vg.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
A suspected burglar has been charged in connection with the death of a great-grandmother following a break-in at her north London home.
Rose Smith, 75, died in hospital 24 hours after officers were called to reports of an aggravated burglary in Tollington Park, Finsbury Park, at around 9.20pm on Aug 11.
An 81-year-old man was also taken to hospital but was discharged the next day.
On Monday, Jeffrey Dean Rose, 46, of Apsley Close, North Harrow, was charged with manslaughter and aggravated burglary with intent.
Ms Smith’s family said she was a “truly wonderful, outgoing woman who was loved by so many people”.
“This is the most devastating loss our family could ever have imagined,” they said. “She loved bingo, going to cafés with her friends and, above all, spending time with her family. She treasured the time she spent with her children, grandchildren and great-grandchild.
“She was the life and soul of every party. She had a wonderful personality, a big heart and a way of bringing laughter and happiness wherever she went. We want people to remember Rose for the person she truly was – loving, fun, kind, sociable and full of life.”
A neighbour who had known Ms Smith for more than three decades said she was a “lovely person”.
The woman, who wished to remain anonymous, told The Telegraph: “She was very nice. She talked to anybody and she liked a chat. I miss her. She went before her time.”
‘I don’t feel safe. It’s terrible’
On the impact the incident has had on her and the community, she added: “I don’t go out because I don’t feel safe. It’s terrible.”
Sylvia Ryan, who had also known Ms Smith for more than 30 years, said they used to talk fondly about both previously being dinner ladies.
“She was a lovely lady – very chatty and joking,” she said. “When [she and her husband] were out on the steps, we’d always have a good conversation.
“I can’t believe that this has happened. I still can’t believe she’s gone. I can’t see why anyone would want to break into their home.”
Ms Ryan’s daughter told her “something had happened” on the evening of Aug 11 at Ms Smith’s address. When she looked outside, she could see Ms Smith’s body near the front door.
John Dyer, 62, a fellow neighbour, paid tribute to Ms Smith as a “good person” who once helped him when he collapsed in his front garden.
Speaking about the couple, the retired decorator said: “They seem like good people getting on with their lives.”
summary: A 46-year-old man has been charged with manslaughter and aggravated burglary following a break-in at a north London home. The incident resulted in the death of 75-year-old Rose Smith, who passed away in the hospital 24 hours after police responded to the scene. An 81-year-old man was also hospitalized during the incident and discharged the following day.
key_points: Jeffrey Dean Rose has been charged with manslaughter and aggravated burglary with intent.
The incident occurred following a break-in at a home in Tollington Park, Finsbury Park, on August 11.
Rose Smith, 75, died in the hospital 24 hours after the aggravated burglary was reported.
An 81-year-old man was also taken to the hospital and discharged the next day.

title: Autistic boy killed after leaping from window, inquest finds
author: Thomas Magill
content:
![A tall beige tower block sits just behind a child's playground.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/3f0c/live/856dd2d0-9a59-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Aalim Ahmed fell from the 15th floor of Jacobs House
- Published
A coroner has concluded that a five-year-old boy died after he leapt from the 15th floor of a tower in the belief he could fly, owing to his autism and inability to assess risk.
Aalim Ahmed died instantly when he fell from a kitchen window, which could tilt and turn, at a residential block in Plaistow, east London, on 16 May 2024.
Contrasting accounts about the condition of the windows were heard at the inquest into the boy's death.
Delivering a narrative conclusion, assistant coroner Ian Wade said that while the window was "compromised", there was "no compelling reason why a landlord should've considered that placing this little boy on the 15th floor was inappropriate".
The inquest had heard that an engineer sent by Newham Council in December 2023 to carry out an inspection and look at overhauling the windows and handles, found they were functioning when he saw them.
In contrast, the boy's mother, Sahra Osman, had a list of complaints spanning several months that included her fears the windows were opening too wide and she did not have a key, the court was told.
She previously said she was "horrified" when Newham Council put them in the top-floor flat, which needed repairs, and said the authority "could have prevented this tragic thing from happening".
The council was exonerated from culpability by the inquest.
In a statement, councillor John Gray from Newham Council said: "This was a tragic accident which resulted in the heartbreaking death of a young five-year-old child.
"Our thoughts continue to be with Aalim's family and friends during this incredibly difficult time.
"We are grateful to the coroner Ian Wade KC for his thorough and fair hearing of the facts of this case, which have at times been very difficult to hear and revisit.''
Sitting at East London Coroner's Court, the assistant coroner said the windows "were not used appropriately".
He said: "Aalim was an active five-year-old boy who suffered from a diagnosed condition called autism, such as to render him incapable of making reliable judgments about his personal safety and abilities.
"In the early hours of 16 May 2024, he awoke and went from his bedroom to the kitchen; he climbed on to a chair and then on to the windowsill of an insecure double turn and tilt window.
"He opened the window and in a naÃ¯ve belief that he could fly or alternatively could come to no harm he leapt from the open window. He died at the scene."
Wade said he did not find a basis for issuing a report to prevent future deaths, adding: "I find there was no compelling reason why a landlord should've considered that placing this little boy on the 15th floor was inappropriate."
He said: "It wasn't the fact that it was the 15th floor that was significant, what was significant was that the windows had become compromised."
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: An inquest concluded that five-year-old Aalim Ahmed died instantly after leaping from a 15th-floor kitchen window in east London on May 16, 2024. Due to his autism, the boy was unable to assess risk and held a naive belief that he could fly or come to no harm. While the boy's mother raised prior complaints about the windows, the assistant coroner exonerated Newham Council from culpability, finding the housing placement appropriate despite compromised windows.
key_points: Five-year-old Aalim Ahmed died after falling from the 15th floor of Jacobs House in Plaistow, east London, on 16 May 2024.
The coroner concluded the boy leapt from the window due to his autism and an inability to assess personal safety, believing he could fly.
Contrasting accounts were presented regarding the condition of the windows, with the mother voicing safety concerns and an engineer stating they previously functioned.
The assistant coroner exonerated Newham Council from culpability, stating there was no compelling reason the 15th-floor placement was inappropriate.

title: Burnham challenges Putin on first trip to Ukraine as UK-Russia tensions grow
author: Maira Butt
content:
Prime minister Andy Burnham has hit out at Russian president Vladimir Putin during his first state visit to Kyiv, amid mounting tensions between Moscow and London.
The British leader chaired his first meeting of the so-called “coalition of the willing” to emphasise Britain’s continued support for Ukraine through the provision of long-range SCALP missile blueprints.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that the move would add “fuel to the fire” and “prevent any progress in the peace process”.
“Who started the fire? That’s the question, isn’t it?” Mr Burnham hit back in an address to Ukraine’s European allies on Monday.
“Putin is now hoping he can win through a campaign of terror using ballistic missiles against Ukrainian civilians.
“This can never be the route to victory, and we need to be clear in sending that message. It means doing everything we can all do, and working with our allies as well, beyond this coalition, to dig into our own stocks of air defence... to protect Ukraine from the missiles that are falling now.”
Mr Zelensky and Mr Burnham both delivered speeches outside Kyiv’s St Sofia cathedral on the anniversary of the country’s 35th year of independence.
“Despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine,” he said.
The prime minister compared Ukraine’s battle with Russia to the British fight against Nazi Germany, saying: “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century; you hold that flame in the 21st.”
It marked his first foray on the international stage, heading the coalition of the willing group of 34 countries set up by his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, in support of Ukraine.
Tensions between London and Moscow have been mounting for weeks as it emerged over the weekend that Russia had withdrawn its ambassador to the UK, Andrei Kelin, last month after seven years in the diplomatic post.
The lower-ranking charge d’affaires has taken the lead in his absence, according to an embassy spokesperson talking to The Times.
![President Zelensky has warned his country faces a tough winter without further support from allies](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/24/16/2026-08-24T145934Z_765620695_RC215NAFSFIH_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-COALITION-OF-THE-WILLING.JPG)
The latest announcement of support by Mr Burnham means that the British government has agreed to allow defence firm MBDA to release classified information and blueprints on UK components for the long-range SCALP missile. The weapons are the equivalent of the French-produced version of the UK’s Storm Shadow.
Last Tuesday, it was reported that British-made drones had been used in Ukraine, prompting Moscow to threaten “consequences” for the support. It warned ominously that the greater the assistance that Britain provided, “the higher price it will pay”.
At the time, Mr Burnham doubled down, saying: “This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100 per cent against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin.”
The European Commission, meanwhile, has approved a further €6.1bn (£5.2bn) in financial aid for Ukraine, to be spent on buying defence systems, including air defence, missiles, ammunition and radars.
![Putin has warned that the UK will suffer ‘consequences’ for supporting Ukraine](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/22/19/2026-08-22T155055Z_625699259_RC2Q3NALWC0M_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-RUSSIA-PUTIN.JPG)
The latest aid package came after €16bn of previously approved procurement plans, of which €8.35bn had already been disbursed, according to the EU.
“As Russia intensifies its attacks, we are stepping up to help Ukraine protect its people and defend its skies. Europe stands with Ukraine and we will deliver what it needs, when it needs it,” EC president Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
In other developments in the war, Russian attacks killed three people near Kharkiv overnight on Sunday, according to the region’s governor, while Moscow claimed debris from a Ukrainian drone killed two children in Russia’s Krasnodar.
summary: Prime minister Andy Burnham visited Kyiv on his first state visit to reaffirm Britain's support for Ukraine amidst rising tensions between London and Moscow. During the trip, he chaired a meeting of the "coalition of the willing" and announced the provision of blueprints for long-range SCALP missiles. Kremlin officials criticized the move, while the European Commission separately approved €6.1bn in financial aid for Ukrainian defense systems.
key_points: Prime minister Andy Burnham made his first state visit to Kyiv, marking his debut on the international stage.
Britain agreed to provide blueprints for long-range SCALP missiles and air defense support to Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov claimed the move adds fuel to the fire, following Russia's recent withdrawal of its ambassador to the UK.
The European Commission approved an additional €6.1bn in financial aid for Ukrainian defense equipment and radars.

title: Burnham backtracks on spending housing fund only on building social homes
author: Kiran Stacey
content:
Andy Burnham has backtracked on his proposal to rip up the government’s housing plans and boost social home building.
Ministers laid out plans on Monday to spend an initial £10bn from the 10-year Affordable Homes Programme on a mix of subsidised housing types in England, in line with the Starmer government’s policy.
Burnham previously called for the programme to be spent entirely on social homes, which are more heavily subsidised and therefore more affordable than other types of government-funded housing.
He said when launching his campaign to become MP for Makerfield: “There’s £39bn allocated over a 10-year period … I’m saying that should be dedicated to council homes. Let’s not be coy any more … I’m saying council homes because control matters.”
Under the plans announced on Monday, however, £10bn will be spent helping to build 70,000 homes outside London, about 60% of which will be social rented houses. The rest will be other types of accommodation such as shared ownership schemes and sheltered housing.
London will get another £6bn, which will be allocated at a later date.
Ministers said the investment would help bring the government closer to its promise of building 300,000 affordable homes over the next 10 years. It will be spent by 33 “strategic partners”, who will be guaranteed funding for the next decade to help deliver their plans.
The Guardian has learned that for the first time in the history of the scheme, three of those partners will be local councils, as the government looks to deliver what Burnham has promised will be “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar period”.
Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said: “Growing up on a council estate and raising children as a young working mum, I know firsthand that access to a secure, affordable home can be a lifeline for families up and down the country.
“Guardian readers will know just how important council housing is too. You will know it’s so much more than just a roof over your head – it gives working parents a safe place to raise their family, offers kids the stability needed to thrive in school and wraps a community around those who need it most.”
She added: “This once-in-a-generation investment will help rewrite these stories, delivering the genuinely affordable homes our country needs, getting people off waiting lists and helping families put down roots so they can get on in life.”
Officials say that another £16bn is yet to be allocated, and that social rent homes and council houses will be prioritised in future funding rounds.
Sarah Elliott, the chief executive of the charity Shelter, said: “Today’s announcement puts councils back on the pitch in the fight to end homelessness. By giving local authorities some of the funding and support they need to start delivering social homes at scale again and ramping up the percentage of funds allocated to social homes, the government has laid the foundations for its council housing revolution.
“But there are still underlying obstacles which hold councils back from building. The government must use the autumn budget to finally remove these barriers, like unsustainable housing debt that councils are saddled with, to make the prime minister’s vision of a new generation of social homes a reality.”
The plans contrast with those announced by Reform UK on Monday, which is promising to boost the supply of social homes by evicting foreign tenants and allowing housing associations to borrow more.
summary: Andy Burnham has backtracked on his previous proposal to dedicate the entire 10-year Affordable Homes Programme to social housing. Under government plans announced on Monday, an initial £10bn will be spent on a mix of subsidized housing types outside London, with about 60% designated as social rented houses. Housing Secretary Angela Rayner stated this investment aims to deliver needed affordable homes, while officials noted that social rent and council houses will be prioritized in future funding rounds.
key_points: Andy Burnham backtracked on his proposal to spend the entire housing fund solely on social homes.
The government's new £10bn plan will allocate about 60% of funding outside London to social rented homes, with the remainder going to shared ownership and sheltered housing.
Three local councils will act as strategic partners for the first time in the scheme's history.
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner announced the investment to help deliver affordable homes and reduce waiting lists.

title: Burnham accuses Russia of ‘outrageous threats’ against UK as he visits Kyiv
author: Jessica Elgot; Dan Sabbagh
content:
Andy Burnham has accused the Kremlin of “outrageous threats” against the UK as Russia warned of an escalation in tensions after the UK’s decision to present Ukraine with newly declassified blueprints to allow Kyiv to improve its production of long-range missiles.
Speaking in Kyiv, Burnham compared Ukraine’s struggle to Britain’s fight against Nazi Germany. “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st,” Burnham said in a speech in front of St Sophia cathedral to mark the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence.
“Despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine.”
In his first trip abroad as the prime minister, Burnham will give Ukraine previously classified information on the British manufactured components for long-range cruise missiles. The prime minister is also set to ink a new deal to share Ukrainian battlefield data with the UK’s Ministry of Defence and some private companies to train AI models.
Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the exchange would add “fuel to the fire” and scupper any moves towards a peace deal.
Burnham hit back in an interview shortly after his speech. He said: “Who started the fire? That’s the question, isn’t it?”
During a conference call while in Kyiv with 34 leaders in the coalition of the willing, countries that have promised to help keep Ukraine secure in the event of a truce with Russia, Burnham also urged other nations to help Kyiv secure more US-made Patriot missiles.
He said the coalition was “doing everything we can all do and working with our allies outside of this coalition to dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks”.
Moscow said it would identify and destroy the locations of missile production sites. “Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime,” Peskov told reporters. “Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire, and methodically and regularly hatches schemes to prevent even the slightest progress in the peaceful settlement process.”
Kyiv was braced for another wave of Russian missile attacks as it marked Independence Day on Monday, attended by other European leaders alongside Burnham.
The prime minister’s decision to declassify the information about the UK-made components of the Storm Shadow/Scalp missiles will enable Ukraine to eventually build its own version, though this may take years.
In his speech, Burnham said Ukraine had “endured 12 years of naked aggression, the occupation of Crimea, and now four and a half years of Russia’s full-scale invasion, all aimed at crushing the independence that we are here to celebrate.”
He said: “Russia’s actions have not changed the path this nation is on. It’s confirmed it. You have stood tall and defiant in the face of everything Russia has thrown at you. And you have taken your place as a proud, sovereign European nation, a vibrant democracy with a bright future ahead.”
He said Europe owed a debt of gratitude to Ukraine for its fight. “I want to tell you something you probably don’t hear enough: thank you. Thank you all. Thank you. Thank you for the incredible stand you have taken because we are all stronger for it.”
The prime minister visited Ukrainian soldiers while in Kyiv, including joining them in playing a Smiths song on the electric guitar.
Speaking to reporters afterwards, he denied he was deliberately ramping up the rhetoric and said the decision to provide the new blueprints was a continuation of the longstanding UK policy to back Ukraine.
after newsletter promotion
Asked by ITV News if he was “poking the Russian bear,” Burnham said: “Obviously with a change of prime minister people think there has been a change in policy. Well I’m here to say there isn’t. I’m going to do what our predecessors have done.
“If we don’t take a firm stand, who would be next? It’s right to do this. It’s in Britain’s interest to stand firm.”
Kyiv has said Russia is amassing more ballistic missiles and considering whether to mobilise an extra 300,000 soldiers. The missiles have been used to bomb Ukrainian infrastructure and warehouses, and to attack the capital, causing increased civilian casualties. There is a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors, the only weapon that can effectively counter them.
Burnham swerved putting pressure directly on countries including Spain and Greece to hand over their own stockpiles of the weapons. He said the UK did not “have those systems to be able to hand over but we will certainly use whatever influence we have got. Obviously there are other threats that people are facing. It’s a complicated world right now.”
The UK has also announced it will help France set up assembly lines in Ukraine for long-range missiles, which the French president, Emmanuel Macron, promised last month. It has also previously announced that it will allow Ukraine to launch attacks with British-made drones, prompting warnings from Moscow that the UK will pay a “high price”.
Russia has withdrawn its ambassador to the UK, with no replacement in sight. The long-serving ambassador, Andrey Kelin, left last month after seven years in post, according to the Russian embassy in London. A spokesperson said that relations had “deteriorated to an unprecedentedly low level entirely on London’s initiative”. A UK government spokesperson said the UK’s ambassador would continue in post in Moscow.
Details of the Independence Day commemorations have not been made public amid fears of a Russian attack.
Macron and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, will attend the coalition of the willing meeting by video link. Burnham travelled to Kyiv with the president of the European Council, António Costa, and the prime minister of Luxembourg, Luc Frieden.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy is facing his biggest internal challenge after his former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for the country to hold elections for the first time since the war began. The Ukrainian president has said any poll risks splitting the country and would be “a tsunami for the state”.
summary: During his first trip abroad as prime minister to Kyiv, Andy Burnham accused the Kremlin of outrageous threats against the UK following Britain's decision to provide Ukraine with declassified blueprints for long-range missiles. Burnham announced a new deal to share Ukrainian battlefield data with the UK and pledged that Britain's support for Ukraine would remain firm. In response, Moscow condemned the UK's actions as adding fuel to the fire and warned it would target missile production sites, while diplomatic relations have deteriorated to historic lows.
key_points: Andy Burnham visited Kyiv on his first trip abroad as prime minister to mark Ukraine's independence anniversary.
The UK provided Ukraine with declassified blueprints of missile components to help Kyiv improve its long-range missile production.
The Kremlin criticized the UK's move, stating it adds fuel to the fire and threatens to destroy missile production sites.
Burnham signed a new agreement to share Ukrainian battlefield data with the UK Ministry of Defence and private companies to train AI models.
Russia has withdrawn its ambassador to the UK, with relations dropping to an unprecedentedly low level.

title: Boy, 5, ‘who believed he could fly’ died after jumping from open window
author: Telegraph Reporters
content:
A five-year-old boy who believed he could fly died after jumping from a 15th-floor tower-block window that had become compromised, a coroner has ruled.
Aalim Ahmed died instantly when he fell from a kitchen window that could tilt and turn at a residential block in Plaistow, east London.
His father, Makail Ahmed, rushed from the top-floor temporary social housing flat and discovered Aalim’s body shortly before 6am on May 16, 2024.
Sahra Osman, Aalim’s mother, has described their son’s death as “preventable” and blamed Newham council, saying she had reported safety concerns about the flat on multiple occasions.
summary: A five-year-old boy named Aalim Ahmed died instantly after falling from a 15th-floor kitchen window in an east London tower block on May 16, 2024. A coroner ruled that the child, who believed he could fly, jumped through a window that had become compromised. The boy's mother stated the death was preventable and blamed Newham council for ignoring multiple safety complaints regarding the temporary social housing flat.
key_points: Five-year-old Aalim Ahmed died after falling from a 15th-floor window in Plaistow, east London.
A coroner ruled that the boy jumped from a compromised window because he believed he could fly.
The incident occurred in a temporary social housing flat on May 16, 2024.
The victim's mother blamed Newham council, stating she had previously reported safety concerns about the apartment.

title: UK to help Ukraine build Storm Shadow long-range missiles: Why it matters
author: Federica Marsi
content:
![Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left, and Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham shake hands during a commemorative ceremony in Kyiv, Ukraine, Monday, Aug. 24, 2026, marking Ukraine's 35th Independence Day. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky)](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/ap_6a8c449e56bec-1787577502.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
The United Kingdom is set to share classified weapons information with Ukraine to enable it to produce its own version of the Storm Shadow long-range cruise missile, designed jointly with France, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham visits Kyiv on his first foreign trip as the UK’s prime minister.
Burnham’s trip on Monday, timed to coincide with Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence from the Soviet Union, is the latest show of support on the part of the UK and Ukraine’s other European allies at a time when backing from the United States has been erratic, analysts said.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 3Putin warns Ukraine has opened ‘Pandora’s box’, rejects peace proposals
- list 3 of 3Zelenskyy says wartime elections could ‘destroy’ Ukraine
Burnham described Russia’s war on Ukraine as “four and a half years of Russia’s full-scale invasion … aimed at crushing the independence we are here to celebrate” as he appeared alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a ceremony in Kyiv.
“But today and every day, you prove that they have failed.”
Burnham is also to co-chair a meeting of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, those nations prepared to provide support for war-torn Ukraine.
The sharing of top-secret weapons blueprints stands in contrast to US President Donald Trump’s backpedalling last month on a promise to allow Ukraine to manufacture its own version of the US-made Patriot air defence interceptor, which Ukraine says it badly needs to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.
While the US has provided Ukraine with US-made Patriot air defence batteries and munitions in the past, Trump last month said handing over the underlying technology to Ukraine to be able to independently produce them was “a hard thing to give away”.
The UK’s decision to share blueprints, however, follows a similar move by France and comes as Ukraine and Russia exchange heavy air attacks and Russian President Vladimir Putin warns of intensified retaliatory strikes on Ukrainian economic infrastructure.
Ukraine has stepped up its domestic military production, crafting long-range drones and missiles that strike deep into Russian territory, but analysts said producing its own Storm Shadows will give Kyiv the ability to hit Russia’s strategic targets more efficiently and at an unprecedented rate.
What are Storm Shadow long-range missiles?
Also known as SCALP in France, these missiles have a range of about 560km (350 miles) and are capable of hitting targets 240km (150 miles) inside Russian territory. This is not as far as Ukraine’s in-house, deep-strike drones, such as the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile, which has a range of 3,000km (1,865 miles).
But while Ukrainian long-range missiles can hit “soft” targets inside Russia, such as Wildberries warehouses, Storm Shadow missiles give Kyiv the ability to hit “hard” targets, including heavily fortified, guarded locations that are usually protected by much tougher defences.
Their advanced navigation systems also mean they can be used at night and in all weather conditions.
Last year, the Ukrainian military’s General Staff said Storm Shadow missiles made by the manufacturer MBDA and provided by the UK had been used to hit Russian facilities, including a chemical plant and the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery, one of the biggest oil product suppliers in southern Russia. This year, they were used to attack Russia’s Black Sea naval headquarters in the port city of Sevastopol in Crimea.
One Storm Shadow missile is estimated to cost about $1m to produce, so they are deployed in more carefully calibrated attacks than the flurry of cheap drones that Ukraine already mass-produces.
![INTERACTIVE - what are storm shadow missiles russia ukraine weapon-1726599224](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/INTERACTIVE-what-are-storm-shadow-missiles-russia-ukraine-weapon-1726599224.png?w=770&resize=770%2C962&quality=80)
How easy will it be for Ukraine to build its own Storm Shadow missiles?
Keir Giles, an associate fellow at the Chatham House think tank, said Ukraine is likely to have a good capacity for producing these more sophisticated weapon systems once it has the blueprints.
“Ukraine, under the force of fighting a war of national survival, has been developing a very agile, highly motivated and distributed defence industry, which is far ahead in terms of adaptation to current needs [compared with] some of its Western European counterparts, including the UK,” he told Al Jazeera.
Being able to produce higher quantities of this missile, more than its actual capability, is what could make the difference, he added.
“Ukraine has had to be highly selective in the targets against which it uses its very limited stocks of the most advanced weapons systems,” Giles said. “Russia, meanwhile, has been exponentially increasing its production of drones and missiles, a trend that’s been in place for several years now.”
“So redressing that balance would be a major step forward for Ukraine, especially if it is able to reduce the number of missiles being launched at Ukraine every night by striking at the facilities that enable those launches,” the analyst added.
Has Ukraine been able to produce any of its own long-range missiles?
Yes. Besides its mass production of cheap short-range drones and interceptors, Ukraine is capable of designing and manufacturing more sophisticated longer-range missile systems, including the Neptune and Flamingo cruise missiles.
Karan Vassil, a Eurasia analyst at the UK-based private intelligence firm Sibylline, said Ukraine has also been developing and testing its own ballistic missile systems.
However, the Storm Shadow/SCALP “is a highly sophisticated weapons system incorporating decades of Anglo-French research and development”, Vassil told Al Jazeera. “Licensed production gives Ukraine access to knowledge and industrial processes that would otherwise take considerable time and resources to reproduce.”
Giles, who also leads the Conflict Studies Research Centre, a group of experts in Eurasian security, said Ukraine may well already have knowledge of the design of Storm Shadow missiles but using it without cooperation would be a “slap in the face to its coalition supporters”.
The reason Ukraine is only now getting access to the missiles’ blueprints has to do with politics, he said. “The United States is not willing to supply the interceptors for Patriot missile systems, so there’s a gap in Ukraine’s air and missile defences, which Russia has been exploiting.”
He added: “European partners are taking up the task of making sure that Ukraine can prevail in the war, and a major part of that is ensuring that it can strike into Russia.”
Vassil said British and French willingness to transfer classified missile-production knowledge sets a potentially important precedent for future allied cooperation. “But it remains uncertain whether this will have an impact on Washington’s posture regarding Patriot interceptors,” he said.
How fast can Ukraine scale up production of Storm Shadow missiles?
France and the UK have expressed hope that they can help Ukraine set up a production line by the end of the year.
However, estimates suggested a new batch of cruise missiles of this complexity could take about two years from contract award to delivery, according to Vassil, who added that establishing production will be a challenging endeavour and will most likely continue to depend on a complex international supply chain.
Storm Shadows also incorporate some sensitive US technologies, meaning some aspects of supply or transfer may still require US approval and “it remains uncertain how this will apply to Ukrainian production”, he said.
There are also substantial security challenges. “Missile-production facilities inside Ukraine would present valuable targets for Russia and would have to operate under the continuing threat of Russian long-range missile and drone attacks,” Vassil continued.
“Protecting production sites, dispersing manufacturing and maintaining supplies of critical components could, therefore, become almost as important as obtaining the technical information itself.”
summary: The United Kingdom plans to share classified weapons information with Ukraine to enable the country to independently produce its own Storm Shadow long-range cruise missiles. During his first foreign trip as prime minister, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the initiative in Kyiv to coincide with Ukraine's independence day. This move allows Ukraine to target heavily fortified Russian locations more efficiently, contrasting with the United States' reluctance to share manufacturing technology for Patriot air defense interceptors.
key_points: The UK will share classified blueprints to help Ukraine produce its own Storm Shadow long-range missiles.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the support during a visit to Kyiv on Ukraine's independence day.
Storm Shadow missiles allow Ukraine to hit hard, heavily fortified Russian targets that cheaper drones cannot penetrate.
France and the UK hope to help Ukraine set up a production line by the end of the year, though establishing manufacturing faces significant security and supply chain challenges.

title: Organised crime arrests as police investigate A66 crash that killed seven
author: Pamela Tickell; Philippa Goymer; Federica Bedendo
content:
![Pictures of the two officers. Both are smiling. PC Blades, left, has stubble and short fair hair. PC Clough also has stubble and short dark hair.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/68ab/live/93348dd0-9f24-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.png)
PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough were killed in a crash near Middlesbrough on Saturday
- Published
Twelve people have been arrested as part of the investigation into the A66 crash that killed seven people, including two police officers.
Nine men and three women, aged between 19 and 61, have been arrested across Teesside on suspicion of a range of offences including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.
In the early hours of Saturday, a Volkswagen Passat that had been pursued by police travelled the wrong way down the A66 near Middlesbrough and crashed into an oncoming police car - two PCs and all five Passat occupants died.
Cleveland Police said it was investigating "serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident".
PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and 17-year-old Cole Robert Worthy.
Earlier, Cleveland Police released more details of its investigation into the lead-up to the crash and information about the 12 people it had arrested.
The force said:
- It received several reports of two vehicles "being driven dangerously" on Saturday morning
- The first vehicle, believed to be a Volvo XC60, was seen "ramming properties" in the Middlesbrough area
- The second vehicle, a Passat, is believed to have been associated with this activity
- Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology
- The Volvo has been recovered in Middlesbrough
- Four of the five people in the Passat had previous convictions
Assistant Chief Constable Wayne Fox said the investigation had been "fast moving and complex".
He said: "The events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect.
"We have a duty to respond to, and thoroughly investigate, the serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident and to bring all those responsible to justice."
![Five young men in their late teens and early 20s. They all have similar haircuts, with a fringe and faded back and sides. Four of them are gesturing with their fingers. Three of them extend their thumb, index, and pinky fingers - leaving their middle and ring finger tucked down. One points with his index and middle finger whilst holding a Lucozade bottle. They are all dressed in casual clothing.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/0763/live/9fa0d730-9f34-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
The five who died in the Passat were Jacob Matusiak, Makai Saddington, Theo Ray, Michael Robert Cahill and Cole Robert Worthy
The 12 people arrested as part of the investigation are:
- Three men, aged 24, 19 and 35, all held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group and possession of an offensive weapon. They are in police custody
- A man, 21, held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, possession of an offensive weapon and criminal damage. He has been remanded on recall to prison
- A 30-year-old woman arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and who is in police custody
- A 20-year-old man arrested on suspicion of threats to cause criminal damage and public order. He remains in custody
- A 26-year-old man has been charged with possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs, as well as the possession of criminal property
- Another man, 39, and a 47-year-old woman have been released on conditional bail after both being arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate, possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs, and possession of class C drugs
- An 18-year-old man has been released on unconditional bail after being arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate, possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs, and possession of class C drugs
- A 61-year-old woman has been released on conditional bail after being arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate
- A 39-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of threats to kill and has been released on conditional bail
Watch: Security footage from a house on Lime Road in Middlesbrough appears to show a car being pursued by police vehicles three minutes before the crash
The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has launched an investigation into the collision following a self-referral from Cleveland Police, which is mandatory when someone dies following contact with police.
The IOPC said officers had followed the Passat for almost seven minutes before abandoning the pursuit when the car went the wrong way down the A66 at South Bank.
Ten seconds later at 03:39 BST, the Passat collided with the vehicle of PCs Clough and Blades, who were travelling on the correct side of the road and were in the area to assist with the search for the car.
Earlier, BBC Verify reported that a TikTok account believed to belong to Saddington previously shared videos showing young men driving dangerously.
It prompted the government to call for social media platforms to remove posts celebrating such behaviour.
Cleveland Police said: "At the current time, there is no evidence to indicate that filming of the activities that took place on Friday night and Saturday morning has taken place for the purposes of TikTok."
![A yellow, blue and white toy police car is set among the floral tributes. There is a plastic flower set on top of it as well as a handwritten note. There is a drawing of police officers and the word "RIP" on a piece of paper wrapped around another bouquet of flowers on the left.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/d921/live/01cd5460-9f80-11f1-82a0-8dbe1008b861.jpg)
Tributes have been left at the crash scene including a toy police car
An online fundraiser set up for the officers' families by the Cleveland Police Federation has raised more than Â£500,000.
PC Blades' wife said he "gave his life in the line of duty, protecting and serving others with courage, dedication and selflessness".
Before joining Cleveland Police, PC Blades worked as an English teacher at Carmel College in Darlington.
The college said: "Many within our community will remember Matty as an intelligent, kind and approachable teacher, a valued colleague and someone who gave generously of himself to the young people in his care."
The family of PC Clough described the former soldier as "our hero".
They said he "jumped into action whenever needed" and was "willing to help anyone for any reason".
The family statement added that he "proudly fought for his country to make the world a better place".
Flags at Cleveland Police headquarters are flying at half-mast and Redcar and Cleveland Council has opened a book of condolence at its offices on Ridley Street in Redcar.
Floral tributes can also be left at the memorial garden at the force's headquarters in Hemlington or any Cleveland Police station, the council said.
Tributes for the five young men have also been shared on social media, with many of their friends saying they were "heartbroken" and "lost for words". Balloon releases have been announced in their memory.
Follow BBC Tees on X,, external Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Tees on BBC Sounds.
summary: Twelve people have been arrested across Teesside following an investigation into a fatal A66 crash near Middlesbrough. The collision occurred in the early hours of Saturday after a pursued Volkswagen Passat traveled the wrong way down the road and struck an oncoming police car. The crash resulted in the deaths of seven people, including police officers PC Tom Clough and PC Matthew Blades, as well as the five occupants of the Passat. The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has launched an independent investigation into the incident.
key_points: Twelve individuals aged 19 to 61 have been arrested on various charges, including organized crime group involvement and firearms offenses.
The crash killed Cleveland Police officers PC Tom Clough and PC Matthew Blades, alongside five occupants of the Volkswagen Passat.
Prior to the collision, police pursued the Passat after reports of dangerous driving and property ramming involving two vehicles with cloned number plates.
The IOPC launched an investigation after Cleveland Police made a mandatory self-referral following the deaths resulting from police contact.

title: Organised crime arrests as police investigate Middlesbrough crash that killed two police officers
author: Live Reporting Edited by Francesca Williams; Caitlin Doherty; With Reporting
content:
